summary.title: Efficient and Flexible Integration of Variant Characteristics in Rare Variant Association Studies Using Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation
summary.authors: Hana Susak, Laura Serra-Saurina, Raquel Rabionet Janssen, Laura Domènech, Mattia Bosio, Francesc Muyas, Xavier Estivill, Georgia Escaramís, Stephan Ossowski
summary.type_of_paper: Methods/software with benchmarking and application study
summary.executive_summary: Rare variants are hypothesized to contribute substantially to the heritability of complex diseases, yet rare variant association studies (RVAS) frequently lack statistical power, particularly in small-to-medium cohorts or when variants explain only a small fraction of phenotypic variance. Whole-exome and whole-genome sequencing enable genome-wide investigation of rare variants, but existing association tests struggle when effect sizes are small or heterogeneous. This paper introduces BATI, a Bayesian rare variant association test based on Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation (INLA), implemented within the rvGWAS framework. Unlike prior methods, BATI flexibly incorporates individual or variant-specific features as covariates while performing efficient full-model inference. The authors argue that integrating meaningful biological context, such as functional annotation, substantially improves power. They developed a semi-synthetic whole-exome sequencing simulator combining thousands of real datasets with ClinVar-derived disease variants to create realistic case-control cohorts for benchmarking. Using breast cancer risk cohorts (1000GP and Iberian), they benchmarked BATI against Burden, KBAC, SKAT-O, MiST, HBMR, and demonstrated that BATI achieves power above 75% in scenarios where competing tests fail, including when risk variants explain less than 0.5% of phenotypic variance. They propose using the difference in Deviance Information Criterion (ΔDIC) for model selection, with a threshold of ΔDIC > 10 recommended. Applying rvGWAS to a Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia study, they identified eight candidate predisposition genes, including EHMT2 and COPS7A. The authors contend that combining real WES background noise with real disease variants yields more realistic benchmarks than purely simulated data. This work provides a comprehensive, user-friendly framework for RVAS analysis, integrating quality control, filtering, stratification detection, functional annotation, and multiple association tests. The central claim is that leveraging variant characteristics through fast, accurate INLA estimation enables BATI to outperform existing methods on realistic cohorts. The study highlights that differences between methods are most pronounced at low variance-explained levels, where some methods show near-zero power. Overall, the paper advances both methodology and practical application, offering a flexible testing approach that can be extended in future work.

The study highlights that differences between methods are most pronounced at low variance-explained levels, where some methods show near-zero power. Overall, the paper advances both methodology and practical application, offering a flexible testing approach that can be extended in future work.

Research Context
Rare variants are thought to play an important role in the etiology of complex diseases. RVs may explain a significant fraction of the missing heritability in genetic disease studies. RVs are more likely to affect protein structure, stability, or function than common variants. RVAS facilitate identification of disease loci based on burden of rare and damaging variants. RVAS still lack power when cohorts are small to medium-sized and if genetic variation explains a small fraction of phenotypic variance.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether a Bayesian RVAS test using INLA can flexibly integrate variant characteristics while maintaining computational efficiency. BATI allows integration of individual or variant-specific features as covariates, while efficiently performing inference based on full model estimation. The hypothesis is that BATI outperforms established RVAS methods on realistic cohorts, especially when using meaningful biological context such as functional annotation. BATI achieves power above 75% in scenarios in which competing tests fail to identify risk genes. BATI is particularly powerful when risk variants in sum explain less than 0.5% of phenotypic variance. The authors predict that leveraging variant characteristics and fast INLA estimation will outperform existing methods on realistic WES cohorts.

Methodological Details
The study presents BATI, a Bayesian rare variant association test using Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation. BATI was implemented using the R-INLA project, with R package INLA version 17.06.20. The method is implemented as part of the Rare Variant Genome Wide Association Study (rvGWAS) framework. rvGWAS combines quality control, interactive filtering, detection of data stratification, integration of functional variant annotations, and four commonly used rare variant association tests. The framework includes Burden, SKAT-O, KBAC and MiST, as well as the two Bayesian alternatives, HBMR and BATI. The framework supports rare variant association for genes or any other biological unit such as promoters. A new disease cohort simulator was developed by combining thousands of real WES datasets from various studies with known risk variants. The simulator randomly assigns WES samples to the case or control group and introduces predisposition variants found in ClinVar. Two large datasets were used as basis for the simulation: 1000GP and the Iberian cohort. For 1000GP, half of the samples were selected as cases and the other half as controls. For the Iberian cohort, one third was selected as cases and two thirds as controls. ClinVar was queried for breast cancer risk variants annotated as exonic or splicing.

Procedures And Architectures
Variants with MAF higher than 0.01 in any ancestry population were removed using EVS, 1000GP or ExAC databases. RVAS tests were performed on randomly split cohorts without introduced ClinVar risk variants to obtain comparable significance thresholds. Significance thresholds were calculated for Burden, KBAC, SKAT-O and MiST translating to 5%, 0.1% and 0.01% TIER. For HBMR and BATI, thresholds were calculated for Bayes factor resulting in the same ΔDIC TIER levels. Thresholds were estimated across 10 random cohort splits, using the test-specific median as thresholds. Model selection uses the difference in Deviance Information Criterion (ΔDIC) between the null and alternative models. A ΔDIC threshold of greater than 10 is recommended to reject the null hypothesis. S datasets were generated by randomly shuffling cases and controls, with S = 10 used for model selection. The benchmark study used 100 simulations of risk variants for each gene separately. The 1000GP cohort results are presented in Fig 3 and Table 2, while the Iberian cohort is in Supplementary S9 Fig.

Key Results
Most tests perform slightly worse due to the smaller size of the Iberian cohort (1,167 vs 1,810 total individuals). BATI's performance is stable despite the smaller cohort size. At a low VE of 0.5% and a strict TIER of 0.01%, all methods except BATI show power close to 0. BATI achieves power close to 100% for three risk genes, with a median power of 55%. All methods except MiST identify all risk genes at 0.01% TIER in the 2% VE setting. BATI calls most genes with TIER 0.01% even at VE of 0.5%, and all genes at TIER 0.1% with greater than 80% power. Burden, KBAC and SKAT-O recurrently fail to call BRCA2, while HBMR fails to call BARD1, CHEK2 and PALB2 already at TIER 0.1%. Differences between methods when VE is low (1% and 0.5%) are substantially more profound than previously appreciated. MiST failed to identify any risk gene at low VE or low TIER thresholds. Burden, KBAC and SKAT-O fail to predict the same genes at 0.5% VE, namely BRCA2, BARD1 and CHEK2. BATI outperforms existing RVAS test methods on realistic WES cohorts using real disease variants in 8 breast cancer risk genes. Applying rvGWAS to a Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia study identified eight candidate predisposition genes, including EHMT2 and COPS7A.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
BATI strongly benefits from the inclusion of variant characteristics as covariates. BATI's gain in power is significant when risk genes contain mostly loss-of-function variants. BATI still performs at least as good as other methods when testing genes containing mostly missense variants. Leveraging variant characteristics and fast, accurate INLA estimation enables BATI to outperform existing methods. BATI represents a flexible testing approach that can be further extended and enhanced in the future. Combining real WES background noise with real disease variants yields more realistic benchmarks than purely simulated data. The use of random causal variants hampers benchmarking of methods that leverage characteristics of causal disease variants. It is likely beneficial to combine Burden- and SKAT-type methods with completely different approaches to compensate for weaknesses.

Contradictions And Limitations
MiST showed favorable results on purely artificial benchmark sets but performed poorly on realistic WES cohorts. MiST's poor performance is likely due to an issue with zero-inflated p-values caused by inappropriate handling of low variant counts. The benchmark relies on semi-synthetic data, which may not fully capture real-world complexity. The study focuses on breast cancer risk genes, limiting generalizability to other diseases. The Iberian cohort is smaller, which may affect comparability of results. The exact random seed for simulations is not reported, which could affect reproducibility. The ΔDIC threshold of greater than 10 is a rule of thumb, and simulations were suggested for evaluation.

BATI achieves power above 75% in scenarios in which competing tests fail to identify risk genes. BATI calls most genes with TIER 0.01% even at VE of 0.5%. BATI strongly benefits from the inclusion of variant characteristics as covariates. BATI still performs at least as good as other methods when testing genes containing mostly missense variants. BATI represents a flexible testing approach that can be further extended and enhanced in the future.
Semi-synthetic benchmark cohorts combining real WES background noise with real disease variants provide more realistic benchmarks than purely simulated data. Simulated variant data is well-known to lack the complexity and noise-level of real data. The use of random causal variants hampers the benchmarking of methods that leverage characteristics of causal disease variants. Here we combined real WES cohorts, representing realistic background noise, with real disease variants. The benchmark still relies on simulations, which may not fully capture real-world complexity. Future benchmark studies should incorporate realistic noise and functional impact profiles.
Differences between RVAS methods are most pronounced at low variance-explained levels, where some methods show near-zero power. Differences between methods when VE is low (1% and 0.5%) are substantially more profound than previously appreciated. Some methods show strongly fluctuating success rates for different genes and close to zero power at VE of 0.5%. At a low VE of 0.5% and a strict TIER of 0.01%, all methods except BATI show power close to 0. All methods except MiST identify all risk genes at 0.01% TIER in the 2% VE setting. Method selection is critical for studies with small effect sizes.

Data And Code Availability
The rvGWAS framework is presented as an integrated tool for RVAS analysis.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Thresholds were estimated across 10 random cohort splits, using the test-specific median as thresholds. Results are mostly similar in the benchmark using the Iberian cohort. BATI's performance is stable despite the smaller cohort size.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is BATI, a Bayesian rare variant association test using INLA that flexibly integrates variant characteristics as covariates within the rvGWAS framework. 2. The strongest evidence is that BATI achieves power close to 100% for three risk genes at VE of 0.5% and TIER of 0.01%, while other methods show power close to 0. 3. The future path is to extend and enhance BATI as a flexible testing approach, potentially combining different method types to compensate for weaknesses.
